title: Pot-au-Feu
subtitle: Classic French boiled beef and vegetable broth
excerpt: France's most comforting dish: a slowly simmered pot of beef and vegetables that produces both a beautifully clear, deeply savoury broth and tender sliced meat with marrow bones. Served in two courses.

recipe.sourceNotes: Pot-au-feu (literally 'pot on the fire') is one of the oldest and most fundamental dishes of French cuisine, described by some food writers as the dish that defines French cooking itself. It consists of beef (typically two or three cuts of different textures: a braising cut, a boiling cut, and marrow bones) simmered at a very gentle, barely trembling temperature for three or more hours with vegetables and a bouquet garni. The dish is served in two courses: the clear broth first (often with toasted bread and Gruyère), and then the meat and vegetables with condiments including cornichons, coarse salt, and horseradish or mustard. The secret to the clear broth is skimming meticulously during the first hour and maintaining a very gentle simmer rather than a rolling boil.

content.text: The simmer must be barely trembling; a rolling boil clouds the broth irreparably and toughens the meat. Skim diligently during the first 30 to 45 minutes as the grey scum rises; after that, the broth should become clear. The vegetables are added in stages so they do not overcook.

content.text: Place the beef in a very large pot. Cover with cold water. Bring to a boil. Drain and rinse the meat and the pot; this removes impurities and gives a clearer broth. Return the meat to the pot and cover again with cold water.

Bring slowly to a very gentle simmer. Skim thoroughly for 30 minutes. Add the onion with cloves, carrots, celery, leek bundle, turnip, bay, thyme, peppercorns, and salt. Simmer very gently for 2 hours 30 minutes.

Add the potatoes and simmer for 30 minutes more. Remove the meat and slice. Strain the broth through a fine sieve. Serve the broth first in bowls, then the sliced beef and vegetables with mustard, cornichons, and coarse salt.
